summary: Describes a way to represent Sieve email filtering scripts as XML, so that XML tools can be used to manipulate them. It also adds elements with no Sieve equivalent, meant for graphical editors to label and group parts of a script. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Mail sorting rules written in a special language get a second form in a tidy, labeled format, so a program with buttons can show and edit them.

questions: how to edit sieve with a gui
how to represent sieve in xml
subtitle: A way to write Sieve mail filters as XML, plus extra elements that let graphical editors group and label rules.

tldr.problem: Sieve scripts are plain text in a special syntax, which is awkward for tools and user interfaces that already work well with XML. Sieve also has no way to say how a script should be displayed.
tldr.mechanism: Each Sieve command, test and argument maps to an XML element (control, action, test, str, num, list, tag, comment), and display directives (displayblock, displaydata) carry interface hints that are saved in Sieve as specially structured comments.
tldr.outcome: XML tools and graphical editors can create and edit Sieve scripts, and the display information survives conversion back to normal Sieve. It is meant for manipulating scripts, not as a storage format.

facts.label: Only attribute on control and action

today: RFC 5784 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains the definition of the XML form of Sieve scripts it describes.

sections.title: Why Sieve Needs an XML Form
sections.content:
Sieve (RFC 5228) is a language for filtering email at or around the time of final delivery. It can run in a mail client or on a server and is meant to be manipulated by many different user interfaces.

Many user interface environments already have strong tools for XML. The obvious approach is to map a Sieve script to XML, possibly on a separate back-end system, edit the XML, and convert it back. Because that conversion may happen on a different system, a common XML representation lets different front ends work with different back ends.

The RFC states a goal: the XML form must handle Sieve extensions without schema changes. The XML-to-Sieve converter needs no changes for new extensions. The Sieve-to-XML converter only needs changes when new control commands appear, which the RFC calls a rare event. The XML form is not an alternate storage format for Sieve.
sections.eli5: Imagine a recipe written in a secret code. Writing it again in a format that every kitchen gadget understands lets gadgets show and change it, and it can still be turned back into the code.

sections.title: How Sieve Is Structured
sections.content:
Sieve syntax is entirely structural and has no reserved words. A script is a series of commands. Each command has an identifier, zero or more arguments, an optional test or test-list, and an optional block of more commands. Commands split into controls (such as if, stop and require) and actions (such as discard and fileinto), though the grammar itself cannot tell them apart.

A test is an identifier followed by arguments, and possibly other tests. Tests cannot be followed by a command block. Arguments are string lists, whole numbers or tags, where a tag is an identifier preceded by a colon.

Extensions can add controls, actions, tests and arguments. At the time of writing only one extension, foreverypart (RFC 5703), had added new controls, so the RFC expects new controls to be rare. Comments are allowed between lexical elements and are used to hold meta-data, so they must be kept in the XML.
sections.eli5: A filter is a list of instructions, like "if the letter is from Grandma, put it in the special box." Some words steer the instructions (if, stop) and some do the work (put in a box, throw away).

sections.title: The XML Representation
sections.content:
Controls and actions become control and action elements. The command identifier goes in a name attribute, the only attribute allowed on them. Arguments, tests, test-lists and nested command blocks are nested elements. The RFC avoids naming the element after the command because that would force schema changes for each extension.

Tests are test elements with a name attribute. Arguments are str, num and tag elements, with the value as element text and no quotes or other Sieve punctuation. A string list becomes a list element holding one or more str elements, which keeps the difference between a single string and a one-string list. A processor MUST preserve whitespace in str content. A nested command block is just the control or action elements inside the outer element, with no block element.

Converting Sieve to XML requires telling controls from actions, which is done with a list of known controls. At the time of writing that list is if, stop and require from RFC 5228, and foreverypart and break from RFC 5703. Unknown controls are treated as actions and still round-trip.

Sieve comments, both hash and bracketed, map to a comment element, so the distinction between them is lost. XML comments are not used because some XML tools make comment nodes inconvenient to reach. Comments sit between commands and inside test elements. Because of XML Schema limits, a comment directly inside a command goes in a preamble or postamble element.
sections.eli5: Every piece of a rule gets its own labeled box: a box for the rule, a box for the condition, a box for each word. Nesting boxes show what belongs to what.

sections.title: Display Directives
sections.content:
Graphical interfaces often need meta-data the Sieve language cannot hold: a script name, whether it is enabled, or the order of its parts. They also like to group related statements, such as those that together make a vacation responder or a blacklist, so they can be managed as one object. Sieve has no mechanism for this, and support is implementation specific, usually done by imposing structure on comments.

The preferred way to add such information is XML in foreign namespaces, placed wherever a comment element could appear. The alternative is two directives. The displayblock element encloses any number of Sieve statements at any level, is semantically meaningless to the script, and allows arbitrary attributes, for example a name, group or order. The displaydata element holds any number of arbitrary child elements for complex data, such as a natural-language description of the script.

Editors MAY use these constructs and MAY preserve them during an editing session. The RFC also warns that extra XML written by different front ends will not necessarily interoperate.
sections.eli5: A sticky note on a rule saying "show this one first" or "this belongs with the vacation rules." The mail sorter ignores the note, but the program with buttons uses it.

sections.title: Structured Comments and Validation
sections.content:
To keep display information when a script goes back to normal Sieve, three structured comment conventions are used. Foreign-namespace XML goes in bracketed comments starting /* [/ and ending /] */. The content of displaydata goes between /* [| and |] */. A displayblock starts with /* [*, which lists its attribute names and values, and ends with *] */. Processors MUST preserve the extra information and SHOULD use this format.

One catch: a */ inside the content would end the comment early. Editors SHALL NOT put */ in displayblock, displaydata or foreign markup, and processors MAY treat such documents as invalid.

A processor MAY validate documents against a schema and reject non-conforming ones. For documents it accepts, any markup it cannot understand from this specification MAY be discarded. Example XML Schema and Relax NG schemas are in the appendices.
sections.eli5: When the rules go back into the old format, the sticky notes are tucked inside comments, which the mail sorter skips. The one rule is that a note cannot contain the symbol that ends a comment.

sections.title: The Extended Example and Appendices
sections.content:
Appendix A converts the example script from Section 9 of RFC 5228 into XML, with its comments, if/elsif/else chain and fileinto actions. It then shows the same script wrapped in four displayblock elements with names such as "File filter list mail", an order from 1 to 4, a group and enable="true". Since displayblocks are semantically null, they can group an elsif or else that is tied to statements in other groups. The regular Sieve form of the same script uses the structured comments. The appendix also shows a natural-language interpretation embedded through a separate namespace and through displaydata.

Appendices B and C are informative: an XML Schema and a Relax NG compact schema. Most complex elements allow elements from other namespaces, displaydata can hold arbitrary XML, and displayblock allows arbitrary attributes. Appendix D is a stylesheet that converts the XML back to regular Sieve, turning foreign content, displaydata and displayblock into structured comments.
sections.eli5: The back of the document shows a whole worked example, plus rulebooks and a translator recipe for checking and converting the labeled format.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Any valid Sieve script can be represented in XML, so all the security considerations of Sieve and its extensions apply. XML brings its own risks, which Section 7 of RFC 3470 discusses. A Sieve editor must be trusted to do what the user specifies, and that trust extends to the components that convert to and from XML.

Other namespaces, displayblock and displaydata can carry arbitrary data, possibly entire scripts and other executable content in languages other than Sieve. That material has its own security considerations, which the RFC leaves out of scope.

For IANA, the RFC registers the XML namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:sieve under the procedures of RFC 3688, with the IETF Sieve working group as registrant contact.
sections.eli5: A helper who rewrites your rules must be trusted, and sticky notes could hide extra instructions, so you should be careful what you accept.

viz.caption: SIEVE TO XML, FROM THE RFC

data.title: Sieve and its XML form
data.code:
Sieve:
  require "fileinto";
  if true {stop;}

XML:
  <control name="require"><str>fileinto</str></control>
  <control name="if">
   <test name="true"/><control name="stop"/>
  </control>
